supportedClaims.claim: Human-driven and robot vehicles will coexist during the transition to autonomous driving. Congestion motivates more efficient mixed-traffic control.
supportedClaims.caution: The slide gives 43 h and $771 for 2024 US congestion, while speaker notes say $700. No explicit primary citation is embedded. Omit the numeric cost claim unless independently sourced. The cited potential for collision reduction is background, not this study’s measured outcome.

supportedClaims.claim: Prior mixed-traffic studies often use small networks or isolated intersections; network interactions and staged transition from signalized to autonomous intersection management need investigation.
supportedClaims.caution: No specific existing algorithm names, references, quantitative road-network sizes, or matched benchmark results are provided in this part of the deck. Do not claim all prior work is single-intersection.

supportedClaims.claim: Fourteen intersections in Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA, with both human-driven and robot vehicles; mixed control compared with traffic signal control. SUMO is explicit in speaker notes.
supportedClaims.caution: The map is a simulated study setting, not a field deployment.

supportedClaims.claim: Human-driven vehicles use the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM). Robot vehicles also use IDM away from intersections; near an intersection they switch to an RL policy. Observing local traffic, they choose binary Stop or Go. Policy trained with Rainbow DQN.
supportedClaims.caution: Thirty-metre control zone, shared-policy architecture, queue/wait/occupancy state details, reward formulas, and 1,000 training iterations are paper-supported existing site details; they are not specified in these PPT slides.

supportedClaims.claim: Five mixed configurations: 2U + 12S, 4U + 10S, 6U + 8S, 8U + 6S, 10U + 4S. U denotes unsignalized, RV-managed intersections; S denotes signalized intersections.
supportedClaims.caution: Fully signalized 0U + 14S numeric baseline and evaluation-window details come from existing paper tables/protocol. Slide 19 states the monotonic-improvement hypothesis, not a generally established rule.

supportedClaims.claim: Robot-vehicle penetration spans 40%–80%; figure x axes show 40%, 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%.
supportedClaims.caution: Do not imply the endpoints 0% and 100% in the conceptual background slide were experimentally evaluated.

supportedClaims.claim: Average waiting time W is mean motionless time per vehicle within the control zone; lower is better. Vehicle throughput Q counts vehicles arriving at their destinations; higher is better. Figure 21 axis uses vehicles per 500 seconds.
supportedClaims.caution: Network destination-arrival Q is not interchangeable with individual intersection pass-through counts. Existing complete table notes must remain.

supportedClaims.claim: Higher RV penetration generally improves waiting time and throughput in the plotted settings. Four plots show 8U + 6S (a,b) and 4U + 10S (c,d), with TL as fully signalized baseline.
supportedClaims.caution: Curves are not strictly monotonic. For example 8U + 6S waiting rises from 40% to 50% and 60% to 70%; throughput likewise has nonmonotonic intervals. Avoid “steadily,” “all configurations,” and “consistent improvement” from overstrong speaker notes.

supportedClaims.claim: Benefits vary across the 14 intersections; bar panels compare 50% and 80% RV penetration.
supportedClaims.caution: Ours is a per-intersection minimum across configurations, not one deployable configuration. Slide says nine improved intersections at 50%, conflicting with complete table minimum count ten. Do not republish nine without resolving.

supportedClaims.claim: The results motivate combining vehicle-level RL with remaining traffic signals as a potential staged transition strategy.
supportedClaims.caution: Replace “prove our hypothesis” and automatic monotonic benefit with conditional evidence limited to this SUMO network.

problem.title: A transition with people still in the loop.
problem.text: Autonomous vehicles will share urban streets with human drivers for years. The control problem is therefore a mixed one: how can robot vehicles improve traffic flow while conventional traffic signals remain part of the network?

existingWork.title: Beyond an isolated intersection.
existingWork.text: Much mixed-traffic control research has studied individual intersections or small networks. Decisions that work locally do not automatically resolve queues and vehicle interactions across a larger urban network.

gap.title: How should vehicle control and traffic signals coexist?
gap.text: The study asks how a network performs as selected intersections move from signalized control to management by robot vehicles, while the vehicle fleet remains mixed. The transition must be evaluated at both network and individual-intersection scales.

method.title: Observe local traffic. Decide Stop or Go.
method.text: Each robot vehicle uses local traffic information to select a binary action through a policy trained with Rainbow DQN. Human-driven vehicles follow the Intelligent Driver Model; robot vehicles follow the same model away from intersections and switch to RL in the control zone.

experiments.title: Two transition choices, one 14-intersection network.
experiments.text: In a SUMO model of Colorado Springs, the study varies both the share of robot vehicles and the number of unsignalized intersections. Five mixed-control configurations are evaluated at robot-vehicle rates from 40% to 80% and compared with the fully signalized baseline.

results.title: Higher participation helps; configuration still matters.
results.text: The plotted cases generally improve as robot-vehicle penetration rises, but gains are not monotonic and are not shared equally by every intersection. The full paper tables identify which combinations reduce waiting time, increase destination arrivals, or produce a trade-off.

conclusion.title: A staged transition, supported by simulation.
conclusion.text: The results support mixed intersection management as a potential route toward more efficient traffic. They also show why replacing more signals is not a sufficient strategy on its own: the network configuration and robot-vehicle penetration must be considered together.

numericPolicy: No new experimental numeric values added. PPT supplies 14 intersections, five U/S configurations, five 40–80% RV rates, binary actions, and 500-second plot units. Exact headline numbers and counterexamples are preserved from existing published-paper Tables I–II in site.json. Congestion cost numbers and disputed 50% count are not in the proposed narrative.
